title: Equations
html:
Equations

Model version 6 (what changed in each version).

Every rule of the experiment as a formula, in the order a run uses them. Each formula has one line saying what it does, and is worked out on the small tree below. The simulation uses all of them; the AI-model tests use the same rules, except where section 12 says otherwise. The same ideas in words: How it works. Full definitions: the design.

The example tree

  • This tree follows the parents-required rule (section 3.2); the definitions in sections 1 and 2 hold for any idea graph, and section 3.1 generates graphs of any shape.
  • Ideas are the circles in the tree. Every idea is the same kind of thing; they differ only in their level, chance of success, bounty and links. An idea with a bounty is what other pages call a target.
  • Arrows go from a parent to the idea built on it. The number on an arrow is the link weight. Credit flows the other way, against the arrows.
  • Levels run left to right, easiest first. An idea before x is one x builds on, directly or through others (y1​, y2​, z1​, z2​). An idea after x is built on x.
  • The letters are the formulas' own: x is the idea in question, y its parents, z ideas further back, u ideas after it. When an example looks at another idea, it says so (for example "for y1​").

One round, as a loop

A run is R rounds (120 by default). A round is one pass through steps 1 to 6: that round's money Budget/R is split among the agents, each makes the attempts it can afford, new ideas are shared or kept, rewards are paid and earnings are updated. The next round starts again at step 1, with the money split by those updated earnings. Each step's box names its section and symbols. Two loops feed back:

  • Earnings shape next round's research money (f). Earnings in step 6 set next round's money in step 1. This happens under both rules.
  • Credit flows back (absorption rates α and α0​). Rewards in step 5 reach earlier ideas, so agents expect more from building and sharing (steps 2 and 4). This is where traditional (α=1) and OSO (α=0.8) differ.

Symbols

Grouped by what they belong to, in the order of the sections below. A hat marks an agent's own estimate: B^ is a bounty as agent i sees it.

1. An idea

An idea is anything an agent can try to find: a result, a lemma, a design. What describes one idea x:

  • Level ℓx​: how far it is from the start; higher is harder.
  • Bounty Bx​: the reward posted on it; 0 for most ideas. An idea with a bounty is a target.
  • Work Wx​(K): the expected money, in attempts, to find x for an agent that already knows the set of ideas K. Each attempt at x works with chance px​(K), so the work is about 1/px​(K) attempts once x can be attempted at all.

Work is what ties ideas together: knowing other ideas can make x cheaper to find, or possible at all.

2. The idea graph

The ideas and how they help each other form the idea graph of a problem space. Everything in this section is a property of the graph (and of α), not of what agents do. Section 3 generates them.

Parents. y is a parent of x, written y→x, if knowing y lowers the work for x: Wx​(K∪{y})<Wx​(K). A parent can be required (without it x cannot be attempted: the work is infinite) or just helpful. An idea before x is a parent, a parent's parent, and so on; an idea after x is one built on x. A root has no parents.

Contribution of parent y to x: its intellectual contribution to x, measured as the work y saves, in the unit each model uses. When parents overlap (either one would do, or they help more together), each one's saving is averaged over every order in which x's parents could become known (the Shapley value), so the savings add up exactly to what all parents save together:

ϕy→x​=∣orders∣1​orders∑​(Wx​(parents known before y)−Wx​(those∪{y}))

Link weight: the contributions, scaled so that an idea's weights add up to 1:

wy→x​=∑y′→x​ϕy′→x​ϕy→x​​

How value spreads through the graph. Value entering idea x is split: x absorbs α of it for its author (the absorption rate, set by the rules), and 1−α passes to its parents by link weight, where the same split repeats. share(x,z) is the part that reaches the author of z, where z is x itself or an idea before it:

share(x,x)=α(1 for a root)share(x,z)=y→x∑​(1−α)wy→x​share(y,z)

The shares from one idea add up to 1, so value is never lost or created. With α=1 (traditional), share(x,x)=1 and nothing passes back.

3. Generating idea graphs

3.1 The generator

One generator makes idea graphs of any shape, with three groups of controls that can be set separately. Each idea is a sequence of bits (like coin tosses): part of it is made of pieces of its parents' sequences, the rest is new.

Group Control What it sets Default
Structure levels, ideas per level how deep and how wide the graph is 6, 8
parents per idea how many earlier ideas an idea builds on, on average 2
skip chance a parent comes from an older level instead of the level just below 0.2
Difficulty length L1​, growth g an idea at level ℓ is a sequence of Lℓ​=L1​+g(ℓ−1) bits (at least 1); g>0: deeper ideas are harder, g=0: every level equally hard, g<0: deeper ideas are easier 3, 2
Difficulty follows level t, from 0 to 1 each idea takes its own level's length with chance t; otherwise the length of a level drawn at random (an idea with no parents: that level's number of new bits). t=1: difficulty rises strictly with level; t=0.8: on average, with about 1 idea in 5 off the trend; t=0: no link. The mix of easy and hard ideas is the same at any t 1
Attribution composition κ the share of an idea's bits that are pieces of its parents' sequences 0.7
new bits per idea n (optional) instead of κ: each idea inherits all but n bits, so every step is equally hard at any depth (used for the deep-graph runs) off
Bounties ideas with a bounty how many top-level ideas carry one, of B0​⋅2ℓ−1 2

Building one idea x at level ℓ: it takes κLℓ​ bits from its parents, one contiguous piece from each in equal shares, and adds Lℓ​−κLℓ​ new bits of its own. Write bits(x) for its set of bits.

An attempt. Every bit inside an idea the agent knows is resolved. An attempt at x works with chance

px​(K)=2−∣bits(x)∖bits resolved by K∣Wx​(K)=2∣unresolved bits∣ attempts

Any idea can be attempted at any time: parents are helpful, not required. Knowing a parent resolves the bits the child took from it.

Link weight: a parent's relative intellectual contribution, here counted in bits (the log of attempts, not attempts): the bits each parent resolves inside the child. A bit that several parents contain is split equally among them, which is exactly the Shapley value for this case:

ϕy→x​=b∈bits(x)∩bits(y)∑​​{y′→x:b∈bits(y′)}​1​wy→x​=∑y′→x​ϕy′→x​ϕy→x​​

Example: y = HHT and x = HHTHHH (x took all 3 of y's bits and added 3). From scratch, Wx​=26=64 attempts; knowing y, Wx​=23=8. If x instead has two parents HHTH and THHH that overlap in TH, each resolves 4 of x's 6 bits; the 2 shared bits are split, so each contributes 2+1=3: weights 50% each.

Example presets. Three named settings of the generator, each told as a story (description and glossary), with a full report on the Results page. They are examples, not evidence about real fields: the numbers were chosen by hand to fit each story, not measured. The scaling runs are the systematic test; a preset becomes evidence only once its settings come from a field's data.

Example Levels × width Parents Length, growth Composition What it shows
A deep, wide field 8 × 10 2 2, +1.5 0.7 a generic field with many levels
Narrow stages (drug discovery story) 6 × 9 1.5 2, +2 0.5 each stage reuses only part of the evidence before it; many dead ends
Small and tightly linked (battery story) 5 × 4 2.5 3, +2 0.8 few ideas, each leaning heavily on several earlier ones

Reports made before October 24 used hand-written graphs; they are kept as earlier versions.

What the controls do (12 identical agents, 10 runs; level reached of 6): with the defaults, traditional reaches 1.2 and OSO 6.0. Lower composition (0.2) makes parents help little, and even OSO stalls at 3.9; higher composition (0.95) makes parents do most of the work, and traditional reaches 5.4, because an agent's own private ideas help it too. Longer sequences, more parents or more levels make it harder for traditional much faster than for OSO.

3.2 The Lean problem set: parents required

The Lean problem set's tree (the real structure of the theorems the AI models prove) uses this rule, as did every result on model version 1: an idea can be attempted only once all its parents are known. The example tree follows it too.

  • Chance per attempt falls with the level, once every parent is known; all parents are required:

px​=p0​ηℓx​−1(p0​=0.5, η=0.6)Wx​=1/px​ attempts

  • Bounties sit on some ideas and double with the level (a hand-drawn graph can put one on any idea):

Bx​=B0​⋅2ℓx​−1(B0​=4)

  • Contribution: without parent y, an agent has to find y first, which takes about 1/py​ attempts; that is the work y saves. Parents' savings simply add up, so the Shapley value is just ϕy→x​=1/py​:

wy→x​=∑y′→x​1/py′​1/py​​

Example: z1​, z2​ and y2​ (level 1) have p=0.5, y1​ has p=0.3, and x has p=0.18 and the bounty Bx​=4⋅22=16; the others have no bounty. x's parents are y1​ (1/p=3.33) and y2​ (1/p=2), so wy1​→x​=3.33/5.33=62.5% and wy2​→x​=37.5%. y1​'s parents z1​ and z2​ are equally hard: 50% each. With α=0.8, the shares of value entering x are:

z share(x,z) How
x 0.8 x absorbs α
y1​ 0.1 0.2×0.625 reaches y1​, which absorbs 0.8 of it
y2​ 0.075 0.2×0.375; y2​ is a root and keeps it all
z1​, z2​ 0.0125 each 0.2×0.625×0.2×0.5

3.3 The Lean graph

The AI-model tests use a third kind, described in section 12: theorems and lemmas, with work measured rather than set.

4. An attempt

The chance that agent i's try at x works:

πi,x​=min(1, si​px​)

A specialist's skill is ×1.6 in its own area and ×0.4 elsewhere; only the Lean problem set has areas, so on generated graphs this does not apply. An attempt costs ki​. A success on an idea someone else already published is a duplicate and earns nothing.

Example: a cheap explorer (s=0.5) attempting x: π=0.5×0.18=0.09, about one success in eleven attempts.

Learning from failure (optional). Each failed attempt makes the next one likelier. ni,xfail​ counts i's own failures on x, and nxfail, public​ the failures others made public, which count λ times as much:

πi,x​=min(cap, si​px​(1+gain(ni,xfail​+λnxfail, public​)))

5. Money each round

Next round's research money is shaped by this round's earnings.

Each round the funder hands out the same amount, Budget/R (10 with the defaults). Part of it is split equally among the N agents. The rest goes to agents in proportion to what they earned (bounties, mint, flow-back). f is the part that follows earnings: 0 means everyone gets the same; 1 means it all goes by earnings.

moneyi​=RBudget​[N1−f​+f∑i′​Ei′​Ei​​]

Ei​ is what agent i earned this round, plus a fading share of earlier rounds (Ei​←0.7Ei​+0.3× this round's earnings), so one lucky round doesn't fund it forever. An attempt costs ki​; the agent makes ⌊moneyi​/ki​⌋ attempts and keeps the rest. The run stops when the money is spent or every bounty is won.

Example (f=0.5): an agent that earned nothing gets 10×0.5/12≈0.42; one that earned half of all earnings gets 0.42+10×0.5×0.5≈2.9.

Epochs (optional, since 2026-11-08): the shares can be reset less often than every round. The run's rounds fall into E equal blocks. At the start of each block, every agent's share is set from what it earned during the block before, smoothed across blocks the same way, and it stays fixed for the whole block. E=1 sets the shares once, before anyone has earned, so the loop never turns. Not set: every round is an epoch, as above.

6. The mint

Since model v5 the flat mint is off (m=0) and the knowledge reward below replaces it. The flat mint is kept as an option: every new idea mints m tokens, which flow back like the knowledge reward below: its author keeps mx​=α0​m and the rest passes to its parents (section 7, with α0​ in place of α). A root keeps all of m. (Before 2026-11-07 the mint had its own cited share c, the part passed to the parents; one absorption rate now serves both of a new idea's own rewards.)

Example (m=1, α0​=0.8): when y1​ is published, its author keeps my1​​=0.8, and the authors of z1​ and z2​ get 0.1 each.

Gaming. With chance gi​ an agent spends an attempt on a trivial idea instead, to collect its mint. A trivial idea is rejected with chance θ; if accepted, it earns m.

The knowledge reward. On top of the flat mint, a published idea can earn mbit​ for each new bit: each bit of it that no published idea has yet. It enters x and flows back like a bounty, but with its own absorption rate α0​: x keeps α0​ of it and the rest passes to its parents (section 7, with α0​ in place of α).

rewardx​=mbit​⋅​bits(x)∖published bits​share0​(x,x)=α0​

A trivial idea or a copy adds no new bits, so it earns nothing; publishing first pays, because once those bits are public they are no longer new. By default α0​=α and mbit​=1, in every model; since model v5 it replaces the flat mint, which is off (m=0). On the Lean problem set (no bits) an idea's new bits are log2​(1/px​).

Example (mbit​=1, α0​=0.8): HHT is public; publishing HHTHHH adds 3 new bits, a reward of 3. Its author keeps 2.4, and 0.6 flows to the author of HHT.

7. Value flow

Value enters an idea in two ways, and then spreads through the graph by share (section 2):

  • A bounty Bx​ enters x when x is first published. The author of each z gets Bx​share(x,z).
  • A new idea's own reward (its mint m and its knowledge reward) enters x when x is published (section 6) and spreads the same way, by share0​ (α0​ in place of α).

With neither (m=0 and no knowledge reward, as in the Lean runs now), only bounties flow back.

Example (α=0.8): x's bounty of 16 pays x 12.8, y1​ 1.6, y2​ 1.2, z1​ 0.2, z2​ 0.2 (16× the shares in section 3.2). Under traditional rules (α=1), x keeps all 16.

8. Choosing what to attempt

Each round, an agent looks at its frontier: ideas it does not know yet whose parents it all knows. It scores each one.

Chance of being first at x, when rivalsx​ agents (itself included) could attempt it now:

winx​=max(1, rivalsx​)1​

Agents see only published work, so rivalsx​ counts the agents that know all of x's parents only when all those parents are published. An idea resting on unpublished work shows no rivals (winx​=1): nobody can see who holds it privately.

Rounds until value from later ideas arrives: 5 per level between x and the ideas with a bounty after it (1 if there are none).

hx​=max(1, 5(average level of the ideas with a bounty after x−ℓx​))

Flow-back: what authoring x earns from later work, if every idea after it is found and published. For each later idea u, its bounty and its own reward flow back to x:

Fx​=u after x∑​(Bu​share(u,x)+(m+rewardu​)share0​(u,x))

Example, for y1​ (α0​=α=0.8): x's bounty sends 16×0.2×0.625×0.8=1.6, and a mint of 1 at x would send 0.1, so Fy1​​=1.7. Under traditional rules Fx​=0 for every idea.

What x is worth to agent i. B^xafter​ and F^x​ are the largest bounty after x and the flow-back, as i sees them: the true value times (1+σ0​(1−qi​)ξ), with ξ a random normal number drawn once.

Vi,x​=mintmx​​​+its own bountyαBx​winx​​​+stepping stoneδihx​​αB^xafter​winx​​​+flow-backδihx​​F^x​​​

The score weighs value by the chance of success, with a penalty for uncertain attempts:

Ui,x​=Vi,x​(πi,x​−γi​πi,x​(1−πi,x​)​)

Example, for y1​: hy1​​=5(3−2)=5. A patient agent (δ=0.98) counts later value 0.985=0.90; an impatient racer (δ=0.85) only 0.855=0.44, so foundations look half as good to it.

The pick. With chance gi​ the agent farms a trivial idea instead. Otherwise it picks at random with chance ε, and else by softmax: the better the score, the likelier the pick (Uimax​ is its best score).

P(x)=∑x′ in the frontier​exp((Ui,x′​−Uimax​)/(τ∣Uimax​∣))exp((Ui,x​−Uimax​)/(τ∣Uimax​∣))​

9. Choosing whether to share: where β comes from

β is the share of intermediate ideas (ideas without a bounty) that are published in the round they are proved. It is a measure of how open a society is: 0 is closed, 1 is fully open. Ideas with a bounty are always published.

Two settings fix it by rule: traditional and the other finished-only settings publish an idea only with the target that rests on it (β≈0); OSO and the other immediate settings publish everything at once (β=1). In the settings where agents choose, β is not set: it comes out of every agent's decision about every idea it proves, in four steps.

Step 1. One decision. Agent i has just proved idea x. It publishes x at once if what sharing brings is at least the risk sharing adds:

opennessoi​m​​+mint lost by waitingmx​(1−δihx​​winx​)​​+credit when others use itδihx​​F^x​κ​​≥scoop riskαB^xafter​winx​ψ​​

  • Openness oi​: how much the agent likes publishing for its own sake, in units of the mint (its kind sets it: foundation builder 0.5, free rider −1).
  • Mint lost by waiting: a private idea is paid its mint only if its author later wins a bounty after it, which happens with chance about δihx​​winx​ in today's value. With no bounty after x, the whole mint is lost by waiting.
  • Credit when others use it: the flow-back Fx​ (section 8) the idea will earn once later ideas are built on it, counted at today's value.
  • Scoop risk: publishing helps rivals win the bounty after x; ψ is how much it raises their chance.

Step 2. Both sides depend on α. The flow-back grows and then shrinks as α falls, because an idea receives 1−α of what flows from later ideas but keeps only α of what reaches it. The scoop risk falls in a straight line with α. For y1​ in the example tree (one step before x, link weight 0.625, bounty 16 after it):

Fy1​​(α)=from x’s bounty16×0.625(1−α)α​​+from x’s mint0.15×0.625α​​scoop risk=α×16×win×ψ

Step 3. A threshold. With 3 agents able to attempt y1​ (win=1/3), patience δ=0.9 (δh=0.95=0.59), openness 0 and exact estimates:

α 0.95 0.8 0.6 0.5 0.3 0.1
Fy1​​ 0.56 1.68 2.46 2.55 2.13 0.91
sharing brings 1.02 1.67 2.13 2.19 1.94 1.22
scoop risk 2.53 2.13 1.60 1.33 0.80 0.27
publishes? no no yes yes yes yes

The two sides cross at α∗≈0.72: this agent publishes y1​ when α≤0.72.

Step 4. From one decision to β. Agents see F^x​ and B^xafter​ through their judgement: each is the true value times (1+σ0​(1−qi​)ξ), with ξ a random normal number (section 8). So for a given agent and idea, publishing happens with a probability, not a yes or no:

βi,x​=P(sharing brings≥scoop risk)over the agent’s estimation errors

For y1​ above:

Judgement q α=0.8 α=0.5 α=0.3
1 (exact) 0 1 1
0.7 (foundation builder) 0.26 0.92 0.99
0.3 (explorer, gamer) 0.39 0.74 0.88

A society's β is the average over every decision in a run, by every agent, about every intermediate idea it proves:

β=intermediate ideas provedintermediate ideas published in the round they were proved​

It is the sharing measure on the result cards. Measured on the default field, with agents choosing (α sweep, 100 runs each):

α 1 0.8 0.6 0.5 0.4 0.3 0.2 0.1
β 0.23 0.22 0.25 0.28 0.34 0.47 0.63 0.77

Even with no flow-back (α=1), about a quarter of ideas are published: dead ends (no bounty after them, so nothing to be scooped and the whole mint lost by waiting) and agents with high openness. β rises steeply only once α≤0.4, because the scoop risk is the whole bounty after x, while the flow-back to an intermediate idea is only a share of it. Everything here rests on ψ, which is a guess (see not yet measured).

10. Sharing and its costs

Uptake. Each round, agent i takes up each published idea it does not know with chance ωi​, and can then build on it.

Uptake cost (optional). Taking up an idea costs a from the round's money, while the agent can afford it.

Wrong ideas (optional). A successful proof is wrong with chance e, and anything built on a wrong idea is wrong too. Ideas with a bounty are checked: one resting on a wrong idea is rejected, and the wrong ideas under it are withdrawn.

11. Measures

Frontier: the hardest level published by the end of the run.

frontier=max{ℓx​:x published}

Reach and cost: the share of runs that published the main level L∗, and the money spent by the round they did.

Value gained and return on the money (ROI):

value=x found∑​Bx​ROI=money spentvalue​

Example: finding x for 40 units of money gives value 16 and ROI 0.4.

Knowledge found, in bits: all the ideas anyone solved count, with or without a bounty. Each idea is a sequence of coin tosses; every distinct toss across the solved ideas is one bit of knowledge, so a toss an idea took from its parent counts once. Finding n new bits takes about 2n attempts.

K = \Big| igcup_{x ext{ solved}} ext{bits}(x)\Big| \qquad K_{ ext{published}} = \Big| igcup_{x ext{ published}} ext{bits}(x)\Big| \qquad ext{knowledge per money} = rac{K}{ ext{money spent}}

Unlike ROI, it does not depend on the bounty sizes, so it can be compared across idea graphs. The gap between K and Kextpublished​ is the knowledge kept private. On the Lean problem set (no bits) each idea counts log2​(1/px​).

Example: solving HHT and then HHTHHH gives K=6, not 9: the second idea adds 3 new bits.

Sharing: the share of proved ideas without a bounty published in the round they were proved. Waste: the share of money spent on repeated work (attempts at an idea someone else had already proved, whether or not they published it), on dead ends, and on trivial ideas.

Credit accuracy: how well bounty pay matches true contribution. Contribution splits each bounty won over the ideas in its proof by 1/p:

credit=1−21​i∑​​∑paypayi​​−∑contributioncontributioni​​​

The answer. Rows are compared on the measure fixed before the run. Two rows differ clearly when the gap between their averages is more than two standard errors:

∣vˉA​−vˉB​∣>2SEA2​+SEB2​​SE=number of runs​standard deviation​

12. AI-model tests: what changes

The AI-model tests use a third idea graph, the Lean graph, with the definitions of sections 1 and 2. Sections 5 to 7 (money, the mint, value flow) stay; the rest changes like this:

  • Ideas are theorems and lemmas. The posted targets are fixed; agents add new lemmas as they go, so the graph grows during a run.
  • An attempt works when Lean accepts the proof. The work Wx​(K) is not set but measured: what models spend to prove x.
  • Parents are exactly the earlier ideas a proof uses; Lean records them.
  • Bounties: Bx​=B0​⋅2ℓx​−1 for the posted theorems, where ℓx​ is the theorem's level in the reference tree.
  • Money is dollars, as charged by the model provider, and each agent gets the same budget.
  • The knowledge reward is off (since 2026-11-06; a setting): a new result earns nothing for itself, and only bounties pay, flowing back by α. Lean has no agreed measure of a result's new bits yet; see the knowledge reward in Lean.
  • Contribution uses the money spent to prove each parent, spenty​, as the stand-in for the work it saves (exact only if the parent would have to be proved again from scratch):

wy→x​=∑y′→x​spenty′​spenty​​

  • Choices (what to attempt, whether to pass) are the models' own, not the formulas of sections 8 and 9. Sharing is set by the rules: traditional publishes when an idea with a bounty is proved, OSO at once.
  • ROI is bounty value per dollar.

What is still a stand-in or a guess: the design: not yet measured.
